exam.title: Programming Fundamentals in C - Class Test
exam.subject: Programming in C
exam.scope_note: Deliberately limited to introductory C programming. Narrow scope is what makes high marking accuracy achievable.

questions.text: State the difference between a while loop and a do-while loop. Give the syntax of each, and state one situation where do-while is the better choice.
questions.answer_key: A while loop is entry controlled. The condition is checked before the body is executed, so if the condition is false at the start the body never runs. A do-while loop is exit controlled. The body is executed first and the condition is checked afterwards, so the body always runs at least once. Syntax: while (condition) { statements } and do { statements } while (condition); do-while is better when the statements must run at least once, for example showing a menu before asking whether the user wants to continue.

criteria.description: States that while checks the condition before executing the body
common_mistakes: says while runs at least once

criteria.description: States that do-while checks the condition after executing the body
common_mistakes: says do-while may run zero times

criteria.description: States that the do-while body executes at least once
acceptable_alternatives: runs once even if the condition is false

criteria.description: Gives correct syntax for either loop, or a valid use case for do-while
acceptable_alternatives: any correct syntax of either loop
common_mistakes: omits the semicolon after the closing while - not penalised

questions.text: Write the output of the given program (a for loop from 1 to 5 that uses continue on even values and sums the rest) and explain in one or two lines why that output is produced.
questions.answer_key: The output is 9. The loop runs from 1 to 5. When i is even the continue statement skips the addition, so only the odd numbers 1, 3 and 5 are added. 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

criteria.description: States that the output is 9
Explains that continue skips the even iterations
common_mistakes: says continue exits the loop - that is break

criteria.description: Shows the odd numbers that are added: 1 + 3 + 5
acceptable_alternatives: only the odd numbers are summed

questions.text: The given program contains three errors. Identify each error and write the corrected line.
questions.answer_key: 1. int n = 5 is missing a semicolon; it should be int n = 5; 2. if (n = 10) uses assignment instead of comparison; it should be if (n == 10). 3. The variable i is never declared; add int i; or write for (int i = 0; i < n; i++).

criteria.description: Identifies the missing semicolon after int n = 5 and corrects it
Identifies that = should be == in the if condition and corrects it
common_mistakes: calls it a syntax error - it compiles, so it is a logic error

criteria.description: Identifies that i is not declared and corrects it

criteria.description: Declares the variables and obtains the value of n
acceptable_alternatives: n passed as a function parameter

criteria.description: Uses a loop to test possible divisors of n

loops to i <= n so n divides itself

questions.text: What is a pointer? Explain the meaning of the & operator and the * operator. Write a short example of three lines using a pointer.
questions.answer_key: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. The & operator is the address-of operator; it gives the memory address of a variable. The * operator is the dereference operator; it gives the value stored at an address. Example: int x = 10; int *p = &x; printf("%d", *p);

criteria.description: States that a pointer stores the address of another variable
acceptable_alternatives: holds the memory location of another variable
common_mistakes: says a pointer stores a value

criteria.description: Explains that & is the address-of operator
acceptable_alternatives: returns the location of the variable

criteria.description: Explains that * dereferences and gives the value at an address
Gives a valid example of three lines using a pointer
common_mistakes: assigns the value rather than the address: int *p = x;
